# Introduction

Agricultural technological change is central to raising productivity, strengthening resilience, and securing food supplies, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where agriculture remains the main source of livelihood [@WorldBank2020; @StateFood2022; @Souder2022]. Yet despite a wide array of proven innovations, from improved seeds to fertilizer and mechanization, adoption and sustained use remain uneven. Land sits at the heart of this process: as the backbone of agrifood systems, it supports crop cultivation while providing essential ecosystem services such as soil fertility and water regulation that sustain agricultural productivity [@IPCC2023; @UnccdSites2022; @WorldBank2020]. Land tenure security is in turn widely treated as a foundational institutional determinant of agricultural performance, on the reasoning that it strengthens investment incentives, eases credit access, and supports more efficient use of resources [@Sltmo2025; @Lawry2014]; where farmers feel secure in their ownership, they are held to be more inclined to invest for the long term and to adopt productivity-enhancing technologies [@Abudikeranmu2025; @Selejio2022]. The empirical evidence, however, is far from settled. Some studies report clear productivity gains from ownership [@Eppinger2026; @Kruse2016; @OBoyle2016; @Hien2026], while others find weak or even negative effects, often reflecting market imperfections and institutional constraints [@StateFood2022; @Goli2024; @Ekpodessi2025]. This mixed record raises a question that is basic to both theory and policy: is land ownership truly necessary or sufficient for achieving superior agricultural performance?

Part of the difficulty is that land ownership is not one thing. It ranges from formally documented rights to informal ownership, and further to non-ownership arrangements such as rental and sharecropping; these differences shape how farmers make decisions and, ultimately, how they perform [@Lawry2014; @Rondhi2018; @Lawin2018]. Farmers with insecure or limited land rights often face real constraints — lower productivity, restricted access to credit and extension services, and weaker incentives to adopt improved technologies [@Selejio2022; @Kousar2018; @Ky2025] — much of which stems from uncertainty over future land use, which discourages long-term investment and careful resource management. The pattern is not uniform, however. In many sub-Saharan African countries, customary and informal arrangements can offer a degree of security through social norms and local enforcement, reducing the relative advantage of formal ownership [@Deininger2023; @Nara2021], and in such settings access to inputs, functioning markets, and institutional support may matter more for productivity than ownership status alone [@Deininger2023; @Peters2022; @Nouf2023]. The policy stakes are correspondingly high: through the Sustainable Development Goals, the United Nations emphasises the need to secure land and natural resource rights for vulnerable groups, including women, indigenous populations, and smallholder farmers [@Rights2025; @Soma2020; @Diana2022]. Progress nonetheless remains uneven. In sub-Saharan Africa, customary and statutory arrangements coexist with limited coordination and weak enforcement [@Deininger2011], creating uncertainty in land rights and generating a wide range of ownership structures that shape access to land, investment behaviour, and agricultural outcomes in context-specific ways [@Lawry2014; @Holden2026].

Property rights theory provides a framework for these observations, holding that clearly defined and secure ownership can improve economic outcomes by reducing uncertainty, strengthening collateral value, and encouraging more efficient resource use [@Soma2020; @Diana2022; @Brunelli2022]. In agriculture, the mechanism runs through two channels that are conceptually distinct but empirically entangled. The first is an investment channel, in which secure ownership encourages long-term improvements and the adoption of better technologies. The second is an efficiency channel, reflecting how well farmers use the resources already available to them [@Coulibaly2022; @Abdulai2010]. The investment story is well established; the evidence on efficiency is considerably less clear, and productivity differences often appear to reflect broader structural and institutional conditions rather than ownership as such [@Michler2015; @Schling2024]. Two limitations of the existing evidence follow from this. Ownership is commonly treated as a binary condition, which collapses documentation, the rights actually held, and the mode of acquisition into a single category. And aggregate productivity comparisons do not separate the technology a farmer is able to reach from the efficiency with which that technology is used, so a study may report that ownership matters without establishing through which channel it does so. This study addresses both limitations directly.

Ghana offers a well-suited setting for the question. Roughly 80 percent of land is held under customary arrangements, with the remainder governed by statutory systems [@Nara2021; @Colin2010; @Tenure2013], and farmers operate across a wide range of conditions — from documented formal ownership to informal arrangements and outright non-ownership, and across modes of acquisition including purchase, inheritance, and family allocation. These differences shape the degree of control farmers hold over land and, in turn, how they invest and produce. Ghana has also pursued reforms bearing on both margins: the Land Administration Project (LAP) sought to strengthen land governance, while the Planting for Food and Jobs (PFJ) programme promoted the use of improved inputs and technologies [@Schling2024; @Wickeri2026; @Ubink2007; @Norton2011]. The analysis draws on nationally representative data from five rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey (GLSS 3--7), which record inputs, outputs, ownership status, and household characteristics. We estimate a Meta-Stochastic Frontier (MSF) model, which accommodates differences in production technology across ownership categories and so allows access to technology and efficiency in its use to be recovered separately [@Battese2004; @ODonnell2008]. Matching is applied so that landowners and non-owners are compared under similar observable conditions, reducing the scope for selection on observables to drive the differences we report.

Anticipating the results, we find that land and family labour dominate output elasticities in both groups, and landowners operate at approximately constant returns to scale (`r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$rts$any), 3)`) against decreasing returns for non-landowners (`r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$elasticities$rts$none), 3)`). Aggregate performance differences are nonetheless economically small: matched non-landowners sit marginally closer to the meta-frontier technology (technology gap ratio of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$tgr$none), 3)` versus `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$tgr$any), 3)`), landowners are marginally more efficient relative to their own frontier (technical efficiency of `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$te$any), 3)` versus `r fmt_num(assert_present(objs$eff$te$none), 3)`), and overall meta-frontier efficiency differs by less than one percentage point.

The consequences of ownership emerge instead at the margins of tenure form, and they do not run in a single direction. Documented owners and holders of transferable rights fall `r fmt_num(100*min(abs(c(tbl_num("table4.csv","Owned with documentation","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be sold","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security and sold","c3")))), 0)` to `r fmt_num(100*max(abs(c(tbl_num("table4.csv","Owned with documentation","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be sold","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security and sold","c3")))), 0)` percentage points short of matched non-owners in meta-frontier efficiency, while within rented, purchased, and family-allocated land, farmers without ownership trail owners by `r fmt_num(100*abs(max(unlist(lapply(objs$acq[c("rented","purchased","kinship")], function(x) x$te)))), 0)` to `r fmt_num(100*abs(min(unlist(lapply(objs$acq[c("rented","purchased","kinship")], function(x) x$te)))), 0)` percentage points in technical efficiency. That the sign of the gap depends on which dimension of tenure is examined is itself informative, and we treat it as such rather than as an inconsistency to be reconciled.

Read together, these patterns suggest that ownership status is not, on its own, the binding constraint on farm performance in this setting, and that the productivity consequences of tenure depend on which dimension of it is examined and on how the land was obtained. The implication is not that tenure arrangements are immaterial, but that formalisation alone is unlikely to deliver productivity gains where the complementary conditions — input access, credit, extension, and functioning land and output markets — remain weak, and where non-ownership arrangements already serve to move land toward farmers able to work it. For research, the results indicate that designs treating ownership as a single binary risk averaging away effects that operate through distinct channels and in opposing directions.

In addressing these questions, the study offers an integrated empirical framework connecting property-rights theory with frontier-based efficiency analysis, bridging two traditionally separate literatures. It makes three contributions. First, it moves beyond the simple "own versus not own" distinction by capturing variation across ownership types and structures — documentation held, rights exercisable, and mode of acquisition — and shows that the measured ownership gap changes direction depending on which of these is used. Second, drawing on a large and nationally representative sample of `r fmt_num(N_ALL, 0)` farm households, it decomposes productivity into technology and efficiency components, separating the technology a farmer can reach from the efficiency with which it is used. Third, it provides direct evidence on whether land ownership is necessary or sufficient for superior agricultural outcomes in a setting where customary tenure predominates, informing debates on land reform, agricultural modernization, and strategies for closing productivity gaps.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 describes the data, the construction of the tenure measures, and the features of the survey instrument that bound what those measures can support. Section 3 documents land tenure arrangements in Ghana over the study period and how they have shifted. Section 4 sets out the meta-stochastic frontier framework and the matching procedure. Section 5 reports and discusses the results, covering output elasticities, technology and efficiency differentials, variation across tenure forms, temporal patterns, and heterogeneity by farmer characteristics, crops, and regions. Section 6 concludes. Supplementary tables and figures are collected in the appendix.
